Title: The Patriarch and the Tsar, [vol. I]: The Replies of the Humble Nicon, by the Mercy of God Patriarch, against the Questions of the Boyar Simeon Streshneff and the Answers of the Metropolitan of Gaza Paisius Ligarides; translated from the Russ by William Palmer

Clean OCR after those leaves.
Content note: Nikon's own long reply, written after his withdrawal from the patriarchal throne, to the thirty questions the boyar Streshnev put about him and the answers Ligarides gave them: the abdication of 1658, his ordinations, the tsar's power to call a synod, and his case that the priesthood stands above the tsardom. Palmer's translator's preface and notes, and extracts from the Kormchaya, go with it.

TRANSLATORS PREFACE. 


In a document read aloud at his coronation, and placed 
by his own hands on the altar of God, where it is still’ 
preserved, the Emperor Paul named the Russian sove- 
reign ‘Ifead of the Church This headship, it has been 
said, was alluded to by the late Pope Gregory XVI. _ 
during his interview with the Emperor Nicholas in 1845; 
and the Emperor may, perhaps, have preferred to de- 
scribe himself as an ‘ Ober-politzee-meister,’ or an ‘eldest 
son,’ rather than ahead. But he by no means abdicated 
his inheritance ; and the world is more inclined to accept 
than to explain away the plain-spoken assertions of 
Peter I. and of Paul: ‘I am your Patriarch ;’ ‘Supreme 
Judges’ ‘lead of the Church.’ 

Lutherans, we know, ascribe on principle to the State 
a ‘superepiscopal’ power; Anglicans owe to the State 
their very existence ; and politicians of this world, wher- 
ever the old union of Church and State still lingers, 
think such maxims natural and conyement. But the 
assumption of a State supremacy in religion has been 
resisted successfully in Mngland by the Protestant Dis- 
senters, whose principles of freedom have now spread 
over America and Australia; it is still resisted in Russia 
by millions of separatists; and it has ever been con- 
demned by the,Catholic Church as antichristian, as pro- 
ductive of scepticism and immorality, and, eventually, of 


| 
eer | 
Vill TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE, 


a reaction against all coercive power; so that it isa true 
political suicide. . 
More than this. As the prophet Nathan, by putting 
before David his sin under an allegory, obtained from 
Dayid’s own lips its condemnation, so the ecclesiastical 
act of Peter the Great, being put one hundred and 
twenty-nine years afterwards, as 7f in another case, be- 
fore the patriarchal Synod of Constantinople (the Rus- 
sian embassy also assisting with its good offices), was 
publicly condemned. ‘The divine canons, it was said, 
require that in every nation the bishops should recog- 
nise their primate, and regard him as their head, and do 
nothing without him; while he, on the other hand, is to 
do nothing of importance without them. So, then, there 
must be a personal primate, who, by enactment and con- 
sent of the Church, may be the bishop even of a new 
capital. Then there is a synod, also already existing by 
divine right, consisting ofall the bishops, who ought, by 
the canons, to meet once at least yearly. And if it seems 
good to them that there should be always with the pri- 
mate some of their number as a permanent synod, with- 
out prejudice to the canonical rights of the rest, as is the 
custom at C.P., these will be of might the senior bishops 5 
and wheneyer any one cannot remain, the next senior to 
him, who is able and willing, will come in his stead. But 
that the king should cither nominate the president of a 
synod, or, abolishing both the canonical primacy and 
the cenonical synod, should delegate a commission of his 
own to govern the Church, this is altogether inadmis- 
sible. Lastly, the primate with his synod is ‘to govern 
the Church freely, according to the divine and sacred 
canons, Without interference of any secular power;’ and 
they are to be free to nominate their own officers and 
servants, and to send forth their own acts, though, of 
course, nothing can obtain the force of civil law till it | 


TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE. ab 


‘has been accepted by the civil government; and for this 
reason a procurator of the king may be present at synods, 
to act as a medium of communication, 

Certainly it was a different thing to deal with the 
autocrat of an immense empire, the sole resource and hope 
of Orthodoxy, or with a petty kingdom, which might be 
rebuked for following the examplo of Russia without any 
offence to the Russian ambassador—nay, even with his 
participation, Still it is plain that, if conscience had on 
both occasions been equally free to speak, the answer to 
be given to Peter the Great in 1721 or 1723 was the 
very same with that which was actually civen to the 
Athens Government in 1850, And this later indirect 
condemnation of Peter’s act and institution, of the sub- 
mission of the Russian clergy, and of the recognition © 
accorded from C, P., comes, not from free-church Pro- 
testants, not from Russian Raskolniks, not from Jesuits, 
but from the chief spiritual authority of the Orthodox 
Catholic Eastern Church. What Russian, after this, can 
say a word to defend or to palliate the usurpation which 
has been sect up in his country? His own Church has 
shut his mouth. But will the Russian Government, then, 
eo back ? Alas, no! Governments which have once 
moved towards apostasy do not casily go back; they go 
-on—to destruction. 

Christ himself said. of the clergy: ‘Ye are the salt 
of the earth ;’? and he added: ‘But if the salt have lost 
its savour, wherewith shall it be salted? [tis thence- 
forth good for nothing but to be cast out, and to be 
trodden under foot of men? In these words there is moro 
than a truth; there is a prophecy, a propheey which 
since 1667 has been visibly fulfilled in Russia, 

But Christ suid also: ‘Ile that leadeth into captivity 
shall go into captivity ;’ ‘Ile that taketh the sword shall 
perish by the sword.’ This, too, has been accomplished 


x TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE, 


in history, and nowhere more remarkably than in Eng- 

land, where Ifenry VIII. and Elizabeth led a nation into 
captivity ; and now their successor, the king or queen of 
England, is the only remaining soul whom tho law of 
that nation still holds bound in that same captivity. They’ 
rose up and took the sword against God; and the people 
rose up and took the sword against them, and even actu- 
ally beheaded them; and again the people rose up and 
expelled them, only for claiming for themselves Liberty 
of conscience. They used the sword, that 1s foree, against 
the Chureh, and the people have used force against them ; 
so that now the Crown alone has least power, while the 
lower and less capable part of the multitude has most. 
So, too, has it been, and so will it yet be, we fear, in 
Russia. There, too, the Boyars and the Tsars led the 
Church into captivity. And they that did this have 
already all been destroyed. Their very names and titles, - 
their posterity, and all the institutions connected with 
them, have disappeared from the face of the earth. Mos- 
cow itself has been burned and rebuilt; the nétme of 


d 

‘Muscovy’ is now forgotten; cverything, even the ecapi- 
tal, has been changed. And for what remains, or has 
erown up instead, since the government that now is re- 
tains its captives in captivity, and still holds the sword 
drawn against God, it is probable that the same judg- 
ments will fall upon it also, As it has trampled under 
foot that order which is the salt of the earth (however 
{rue it may be that the salt had lost its savour), so it 
will itself probably be trampled under foot by swine, by 
swine which it has itself blindly reared and multiplied, 

But without pursuing farther these questions, we 
remark that, though all the world see a State supremacy 
now existing in Russia, very few know how it originated. 
Some may think that it was from the beginning a defect 
inherent in the Russian as in the Greek Church ; others, 


TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE. xi 


that it was altogether the work of Peter the Great, who 
trampled under his feet the malcontent boyars and tho 
clergy, without encountering any moral or spiritual power 
of resistance. But that there had been in Russia a gra- 
dual development towards apostasy, like that of Western 
jurope; that, after letters and laws had been intro- 
duced by the clergy; after the unity of the monarchy 
had been formed clicfly through them y ufter an age of 
religious feeling had liberally endowed . the Church, 
—there had followed, as in the West, another age, in 
which the wealth of the Church drew upon her the 
cupidity of rulers and the jealousy of nobles; that hence 
at length there ensued a conflict of principles between the 
secular and the spiritual authorities, uke that which was 
“ried on, in the cleventh and twelfth centuries, be- 
tween the Popes and the German Emperors, though in 
tussia it had a different end; and that Russia pro- 
duced a champion of ecclesiastical rights, holding the 
same place in her history as St. Thomas & Becket holds 
in that of England, or Gregory VII. or Alexander III. 
in that of Christendom at large; and that this contlict 
had already begun and ended before the birth of Peter 
the Great, under is father the Tsar Alexis Michaclo- 
vich,—all this is known to few in Western Europe. 
Nay, even in Russia itself, the memory of that great 
man to whom we have alluded has been hitherto in ‘a’ 
manner suppressed, People know, indeed, that he was 
Patriarch of Moscow; that the Tsar, who, as a youth, 
had shown him unbounded affection and respect, was, by 
the time that he was twenty-nine years old, estranged 
from him, so as to take part with the boyars, who hated 
him; that he retired from Moscow, and lived at Voskre- 
sensk, building a church from a model of the church 
of the Resurrection at Jerusalem, with a monastery 
around it, named the New Jerusalem; that he held his

enemies at bay for cight years; that at length, at the 
suggestion of a Greck of bad character, the Tsar in- 
duced two of the Greck patriarchs, with other bishops, 
to come to Moscow and to preside in a mixed synod, 
which condemned Nicon, degraded him even from the 
priesthood, and delivered him over to be exiled and im- 
prisoned; that he was kept under guard fifteen years, 
and liberated at the request, rather than by the order, 
of the young Tsar Theodore, in August 1681, only when 
he was dying. <All these facts certainly are well known. 
But that which is necessary to give point and meaning 
to them all—though it was on the very surface—is not 
known, 

After an interval of about a century, portions of the 
numcrous documents relating to Nicon’s life and con- 
demnation, and still preserved, began to be alluded to 
or quoted; and as time went on such documents or 
extracts from documents have been published with in- 
creasing freedom, especially during the present reign. 
First, in a.p. 1784, Kozodavleff, who had been Minister 
of the Interior, published a short life of Nicon, by Ivan 
Shusherin, one of Nicon’s own disciples, who, merely on 
account of lis fidelity and attachment, was put to tho 
question and imprisoned for ten years. Ile writes as if 
he were writing the life ofa saint; and the anecdotes 
and sayings related by him bear such niarks of character 
that the reader feels brought into personal contact with 
the patriarch himself. But whether from fear, or from 
some other cause, Shusherin says merely that the enemy 
sowed discord between the Tsar and the blessed Nicon, 
without a word of the occasion or nature of their differ- 
ence, Then Platon, metropolitan of Moscow, who had 
been preceptor to the Emperor Paul, in his ‘Remarks 
on’ the History of the Russian Church,’ exposes the m- 
justice or insufliciency of the charges brought against

Nicon, but he makes a mystery of the cause of his fall. 
So does the metropolitan Kugenius, in his ‘Dictionary 
of Russian Ecclesiastical Writers ;’ so does Mouravicff, 
in his ‘IListory of the Russian Chuirch;’ so does Philaret, 
archbishop of Kharkoff, in his: so, in short, do they all. 
And this is not only from any fear of the censors of the 
press, or of the government; but even in private con- 
versations, even those who are most religious, and most 
inclined to take Nicon’s part, are stone blind as to 
that question which for him was all-important, and for 
which he was ready, as he said himself, not only to be 
imprisoned, but to dic, To say nothing of ‘the Staro- 
obratsi, who have from the first regarded lim as Anti- 
christ for his correction of the church books, and to 
speak only of members of the dominant Russian church, 
some, with Mouravieff, say that he was a mixed cha- 
racter, ‘alternately bright and dark, great and feeble,’ 
a good and an evil genius for the Tsar Alexis and for 
“Russia; many say that he was ‘deficient in Christian 
meckness ;’ others that le was indiscreet, harsh, and 
impatient; others that he was a regular mujik. Thanks 
be to the Professor Solovieff, he at last has given us a 
complete view—the view of ono who had taught history 
to members of the imperial family. According to him, 
then, Nicon was a coarse, unspiritual man—proud, am- 
bitious, passionate, crucl, covetous, cunning, mean—a 
lover of good cating and drinking, &e. Of Shusherin’s 
life he speaks with contempt, as being manifestly written 
by a partisan; and Shusherin himself (whose name would 
in Latin be ‘Stercorius’) he always nicknames ‘Shus- 
hera,’ that is ‘Stereus.”’ But Paisius of Gaza he follows 
as trustworthy. Jls ‘Ilistory of Russia,’ and of the 
‘Reign of Alexis Michacloyich’ in particular, shows 
that he had free access to all the imperial archives, and 
that he was as diligent as a German might have been in

examining them. But with all this, he is no improve- 
ment upon his predecessors they only professed to be 
vat fault, he finds no difficulty, but leads ay ray from the 
‘truth. To justify the Tsar and the beyars, might be, 
for him, a matter of course ; but he blackens Nicon with 
too much zeal; and in that he overshoots his mark. Tor 
no thoughtful reader, though he may be a seeptie or a 
muaterialist, and an opponent of ecclesiastical authority, . 
will accept, unless he be also malicious, Solovicft’s eari- 
ature of Nicon as an explanation. In Russia it ealled 
forth two other publications, by MM. Subbotine and 
Michaclofsky, each of them remarkable in its Way, Of 
these, Subbotine treats Solovieff with profound respect, 
but suggests that his account of Nicon is not quite Im- 
- partial, and that somo documents (which he himself 
appends in a supplement) ought not to haye been left 
unnoticed, But it docs nof occur to him to turn tho 
tables on the protessor, and to tell him plainly that 
either he was very dull if he did not see, or much worse 
than dull if he did see, that Nicon also, no less than 
himself, had a view, for which he was a zealot, and to 
Which any fair and Senerous adversary would have 
sought to do justice before combating and refuting it, 
But the other writer, Michaclofsky, differing entirely 
from Solovieff in his estimate of the personal character 
of Nicon, would fain make of him a hero or a saint, of 
only this can be done without too openly condemning the 
evisting order of things. So he trics to show that Nicon, 
though ill-used, was yet in truth victorious, and, like 
other confessors, overcame by his suffering and patience 
(and this may indeed he truc, but certainly not in the 
sense suggested). For, he says, the synod which con- 
demned him approved his acts: it confirmed his cor 
rection of the church books; it decreed that in clyil 
matters the Tsar, but in spiritual the patriarch, was to

be supreme; and it blamed the practice of conferring 
ordination by ukaz only of the Tsar; lastly, the Monas- 
tery Court itself, Nicon’s main grievance, was some: 
years afterwards suppressed. O, wonderful simplicity ! 
If this were all, Solovieff and Michaclofsky might shake 
hands over Nicon’s tomb, Solovieff’s spite wonld be 
quite unnecessary, and Michaclofsky’s admiration quite 
harmless. But in truth, such is the force of laws and 
institutions, and of social traditions, to mould the minds 
of whole peoples and generations, that the plunest truths 
become invisible, and the most palpable absurdities 
come to be aceepted and repeated as plain truths. We 
are like caterpillars or small insects on the leaves of 
plants and trees, which have their heads turned down- 
wards, and take unconsciously their’ colour from the 
leaf on which they feed. Only in the long run, and- 
on a scale too great for us in our short lives to perceive 
its lessons, the providence of God causes the error and 
euilt of false teachers and of rulers to work out, by an 
inexorable law, its own confusion and its own punish-« 
ment. | 

sut to return, That which Nicon has suffered since 
his death was foreshadowed allegorically in an incident 
related of his boyhood. One day—so writes Shusherin— 
when it was a hard frost, the boy Nicetas crept into the 
empty stove for the remains of its warmth, and there 
fell asleep; and his stepmother, as if not seeing him, 
put in logs of wood, so as to block him up, and haying 
lit them went her way. And she would have got rid 
of him altogether, had not a neighbour named Xenia, 
hearing his cries, run in, and pulled out from the stove 
the burning wood, Ils stepmother was the Tastern 
Orthodox Church, which unquestionably treated him as’ 
a stepmother; and especially the Russian Church and 
hierarchy, which neither supported him when he was

living, nor has appreciated or vindicated his memory 
after death, but has passively conspired with the secular 
power to suppress it. Not ono single bishop, of all those 
whom he had conseerated, stood by him openly and 
manfully, though two or three, while doing the bidding 
of the ‘Tsar and the boyars, may have shown signs of 
misgiving and reluctance. 

ere one may pause to reflect what would have been 
the fate of the Cathohe Church, if it had been all con- 
tained within one empire, and if, instead of many great 
Popes capable of contending with kings and emperors, 
and supported by many other primates and bishops like 
themselves, there had been only one man, and he a sub- 
ject and unsupported. 

Again. It is manifest to students of ecclesiastical 
history, that both in the time of Photius, and during 
the two centurics which followed, and again in the time 
of Cerularius, the act itself of breaking off from commu- 
nion was always determined by political or even per- 
sonal rather than by religious motives. Whatever con- 
currence there may have been af other causes and 
tendencies, whatever occasion may have been given 
from the West—and the selfwill of those who first inter- 
polated the Creed, in spite of the Pope himself, cannot be 
too severely blamed—still, neither the interpolation of 
the Creed, nor the Latin doctrine of the Filioque, nor 
Azyies, nor any other Latin doctrine or observance, of 
itvelf alone, ever caused a rupture, But it was not 
enough that this should be manifest to students of his- 
tory. The providence of God so ordered it that the 
Greek Church cyentually confessed the same publicly 
of herself. As a last act, when the Byzantine empire 
was about to be destroyed, the emperor, with repre- 
sentatives of the four patriarchates, and with other 
bishops, came to Florence; and though in the council 


TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE, xXVil 


they held strongly to io language of their own Greek 
fathers, and wero not convinced of there being any 
logical necessity for the Latin development, they yet 
consented to submit for the future, in the hope of ob- 
taining help against the ‘Turks, Doubtless they were 
mn a great strait: stil, if they had in their consezences, 
and not only in their dtedlects, been convinced that the 
Milioque, or any other Latin eee was a heresy, like 
that, for example, of Arius or of Apollinaris, they could 
not so have traflicked with {heir consciences; and thei 
act was an admission, though, if may be, an unconscious 
one, thatthe demal of the Latin doctrine was not, even 
to themselves, in their inner souls, a part of the faith. 

The people, however, who had long before followed 
emperors and patriarchs into schism, would not now, 
though with the Turk at their gates, follow them back 
for political motives to reunion. ne preverred the 
Lurk to the Pope. And, secing this, the greater part 
of those who had subscribed the union at Ilorence flew 
back from it: and it even came to be a saying among 
them, that God had placed them under the dominion of 
the thane to defend them against the Latin heresy, 

But at this very time we seo a new Christian world, 
as if were—uan empire capable of being compared for 
extent to the Latin and the Greck empires together, and 
Which had always been connected with the Patriarchate 
of C,P.—emerging from under the yoke of the Mongols 
to liberty and to power. What is most remarkable i 1M, 
that this prodigious extension of Christianity from C.P., 
which can scarecly be said to have begun before the ex- 
pulsion of St. Ignatius in A.p, 858, was obtained chiefly 
during those two eenturics of alternate schisms and re- 
unions which intervened between Photius and Cerula- 
rius; and that it by no means stopped short on, the con- 
summation of the schism by Cerularius, but continued

still to spread till a.p. 1240, and even under the Tatar 
yoke, converting heathens, producing apparently saints 
ant confessors and martyrs, founding churches and monas- 
teries, and multiplying miraculous apparitions and heal- 
ings, In connection often with local saints, and with holy 
images and relies. And the hierarchy, on which at C.P. 
the yoke of the empire pressed heavily, in Russia, as if 
escaping from thraldom through its missionary character, 
instructed and rebuked princes with an apostolical free- 
dom, and from the anarchy of mulliplied principalities 
helped them towards a concentration of power, and to- 
wards the adoption of a better law of succession in the 
right line of primogeniture. 

What is the meaning of this? since nothing happens 
without a meaning. Is it, that the Greek Church, 
although she had broken off from the Latin, had still life 
in herself, and was cither (as she herself has always 
claimed to be) exclusively the true Orthodox Catholic 
Church, or (as some now would rather say for her) a 
part at least of the true Church, the true Church be- 
ing divided ? and that though the four patriarchates had 
fallen under the Turk, a third Rome was rising in | 
Moscow to condemn with better success than C.V. the 
‘Apollinarian heresy’ of the Popes? It certainly secins 
strange at first sight that such siens of life and so vast a 
development should be allowed to schism, neutralising 
through the North that lesson which else might have 
seemed to be unmistakably given by the ruin and degra- 
dation of Constantinople. But if the slip of the Church

Question NNIIT, Ts it proper for a bishop to scourge, and to strike, 
and to exile, all which things Nicon did, and was never satisfied with 
doing, both to lay people and to those of the clergy? Answer, I see no 
better virtue ina man than justice and pudience, nor any worse evil than 
anger, We praise Abrabam for his patience, &e.; we honour Moses for 
his patience towards the people who were disobedient and ungrateful ; 
we admire the meckness of Job, Paul patiently endured many labours 
and hardships, of which he himself writes, David endured the ingrati- 
tude of his son Absalom, and ihe malice of Shimei, who followed him 
cursing, and casting stones at lim, ‘Touch not,’ it is written, ‘mine 
anointed, and against my prophets be not malicious.” The anointed are 
all the sacerdotal order, for ‘Thou hast made us kings and priests,’ aecord- 
ing to the Apocalypse. IXings wo become when we master our passions, 
priests when we offer to God all our senses, For Epicurus was a fool 
when he denied that a mau can endure to be patient, or to resist temporal 
disturbances, Rather, on the contrary, he is then a philosopher when he 
endures with patience, And it is not proper for a bishop to inflict such 
cruel punishments; and the bishop who acts otherwise will hear that 
rebuke of Christ, ‘Put up thy sword into its sheath; for all they that 
take the sword shall perish by the sword.’ To the secular prince it is 
given to gird on the sword, but not to aman in holy orders, Seest thou 
not that all the episcopal vestments are garments emblematic of mccehness 
and justice? The efichurion signifies angelic purity, and the bright life 
becoming a bishop; the eyitrachelion is the perfect grace of the Holy 
Spirit from above; the menples are the shackles binding the hands of 
Christ ; the e¢netire is his ligature; the ep/yonution is Christ's victory and 
resurrection, and it is shaped like a sword, having upon it cither the 
crucifixion or the resurrection, in accordance with that verse of the psalm, 
‘Gird thee with thy sword upon thy thigh, O thou most Mighty ;’ the 
palitsa is victory; the sai/os figures the passion and crucifixion of Christ ; 
the oiophorion signifies- the lost sheep which Christ took upon his 
shoulders ; the panagde is the incarnation ; the wiélre is the royal priest- 
hood, <All these episeopal robes signify paticnec, meckuess, temperance, 
and the most precious of all virtues, justice, Deply (to both together)

Question XX V, ILas the Tsar power to take away those privileges from 
the man to whom he may have granted them? ulnswer, Yes; he has: 
for the spiritual law says, ‘Gifts given to the unthankful shall be taken 
back from them.’ Ifo should, however, be cautious how he gives such 
gifts. God, according to the Apostle, has set some apostles, others pro- 
phets: he has not given to one all gifts, that that one should not have in- 
citements to forwardness, and so come to be excluded from his grace, But, 
as Ezekiol says, ‘Thine heart was lifted upin thy beauty, and thy wisdom 
was corrupted by thy brightness: for tho multitude of thy sins I have 
‘ast thee down to the ground ; I have given thee to be made an example, 
and to be put to shame before kings ... thou art become destruction, 
and shalt be no more for ever.’ Milo of Crotona—so strong was he in 
his own conceit-—expected that he should have strength also in his hands, 
and it befell him exactly as it befell Polydamas, who, wishing with his 
hands to support a cavern of rock, was crushed: so Milo attempted to 
rend a tree in twain, but, when ho had only cleft it asunder, Ins strength 
was exhausted, and the treo flying back caught his hands and held them 
wedged in its trunk: and after a time the wolves camo and. devoured 
him alive. Sceing Nicon in the midst of so many benefits ungrateful,

Then he goes through the whole of the New Testament, showing how 
the Iloly Spirit nowhere speaks or legislates without references to the law

anything be done now by Christians, or by Christian rulers and legislators 
(except they be apostetising), without reference to the holy scriptures of 
the Old and New Testaments, and to the divine canons and spiritual 
laws of the Church, ‘This collection of testimonies Nicon marks off, so 
that the reader may pass it over if ho pleases, p, 423 to 463, 

Then, returning to the Code, after recapitulating the preceding argu- 
ment, he argues that, If thy Code enacts such penalties as burning at the 
stake for blasphemy, and death without mercy for treasonable practices 
against the Tsar, as by fraudulent abuso of his authority, by forging or 
corrupting documents or signatures, or abusing his seal, what punishment 
will not thy blasphemy and thy fraud against the King of kings deserve ? 
p. 468. Instead of Christ’s precepts with regard to injuries, the Code 
enacts for clergy as well as laity a graduated scale of retaliations, by sa- 
tisfactions in stripes, and in imprisoninents, and in money, p. 472. Also 
it enacts unequal panishinents, ‘favouring thyself, and all like thyself’ 
(ic, the boyars and okolniks), p,475, It creates the Monastery Court to 
judge all causes affecting the clergy and monks, and their property and 
their people, without at the same place distinctly specifying who ure to be 
the judges in that court ; but elsewhere in the same Code it is said that 
the judgment of the Tsar in all causes between man and man for ull the 
people (no distinction being made of the clergy) of the Muscovite empire, 
from the least to the greatest, is to be given by the boyars, and okolniks, 
and people of the council, and seerctaries, and all the people of their 
prikazes, and the judges, p. 477. This certainly is ‘written out’ from 
no canons nor Greck civil laws, quoting from them, p. 478; then he quotes 
Christ's precepts from the gospel, p. 479. The Code preserves, indeed, to 
the patriarch’s prikaz or court its jurisdiction over his own dyor-people,

but at the same time, the patriarch himself by other enactments is

whoever it may happen to be, p, 484. The Code enacts penaltics against 
such as take from a ‘Tsar's officer his warrant o¢ minute of instructions,

Canon xx, of the Sixth Ee, Council: ‘A bishop in another city

on the 12th day of Hyperboreteus? The gloss: ‘This canon, 
however, has been modified, For canon vill. of the Sixth Coun-

that the synods of the bishops in each province’ shall be held

causes. And if any bishop has ‘bound any with heavy penances 
or with excommunication, of such matters also all the bishops 
in synod shall judge, And they fixed one time for the hold-

VIL. REPLY AGAINST THE EIGHTH QUESTION AND ANSWER, 


Question of Simeon Streshnef’: ‘Can our sovereign Alexis 
Michaelovich assemble that synod? or must it be assembled 
by patriarchal command?’ Reply: But there is nowhere any 
such canon as that kings or emperors should convoke synods ; 
especially to vindicate their own cause, Canon xxxvil. of the 
Apostles: “Pwice in the year the bishops shall assemble them- 
selves! for ecclesiastical matters, and for doctrine. See here, O 
thou Answerer, how the holy canon speaks, ‘shall assemble them- 
selves, not ‘shall be assembled by the emperor, or by any 
other. In like manner also canon y, of the First Heum. Council, 
and canon xix, of the Fourth Heum, Council, and canon i, of the 
Third, and canon y. of the Seventh... If it be also true that in 
old times synods were conyoked by religious emperors, still this 
was by way of request, not by command, as it is now thre prac- 
tice to convoke them by command and compulsion: as also 
here in ‘the Ninth Question it is plain that it is a compulsory 
command, not a request, which is intended.

The ancient Form for the Institution of Tsars contains the 
following notice: ‘There are five insignia properly belonging to 
the Tsar, which the patriarch in consecrating him, at his corona- 
tion, gives. The jirst is the crown, which he places on his head ; 
and its conformation is as it were a crown with a certain: cloud 
over the head, which has four lilies, for a sign that the Tsar is 
to be gentle, of handsome bearing, and god-fearing ; also that he 
is to lead in good order the rest of the people who are from the 
four elements; also that he is to be obedient, mereifal, eracious 
towards the good, and not wrathful, as a lily is among the 
flowers, On the crown there is a cross, in token that he is to 
remember that he is crowned to reign over all the people whom 
the Son of God redeemed upon the cross, The second of the 
insignia is the Jamner with the eagle, which has a eross on its 
breast, in token of this, that he is to bear the cross before all 
the Christians, for the defence of all, and is to be ever ready to 
die for the orthodox Church, of which he is the shield. I*or 
this cause also the patriarch, when he anoints him with oil on 
the shoulders in the form of a cross, says in prayer to God thus: 
“QO Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, sanctify this thy 
servant, that he may be to us an invincible shield against all’ 
enemies visible and invisible, even as thou thyself, by thy most 
precious blood shed on the wood of the cross, didst sanctify us 
and deliver us from all the power of the enemy.” The third of 
the insignia is the orijlamme,' yellow in the middle, with a 
purple or searlet border. The purple signifies sincere affection, 
which the Tsar ought to have towards the Lord God, and 
towards good men; the yellow indicates that beneficence which 
in the mortal body he ought to show to the rest of his fellow 
men ; it indicates also death, with which it is his duty to punish 
evil men according to the law; because the yellow hue, as pro- 
fessors of medicine consider, betokens death, The fourth of the 
insignia is the golden apple, or ball, which opens and shuts; and 
it is filled full with earth, which signifies the death of the Tsar

‘The Divine, having begun to enumerate the five senses, puts

well, since they are an abundant food for evil, and ingresses of

been before shown, We have been forbidden by the Lord our

The first Slavonic Nomocanon—the one used in Russia till its subjugation 
by the Tatars—was a translation from that of Johannes Scholasticus, a copy 
of which was sent to Bulgaria (after the baptism of the Prince Bogoris or 
Michael in A.D. 866) by the Patriarch Photius from Constantinople, 

Johannes Scholasticus, while yet only a priest of the church of Antioch and 
its Apocrisiarius at C, VP., had made a‘ Colleetion of the Canons’ based on that 
code of Chalcedon to which Novell exxxi, of Justinian about the same time 
(A.D, 541) gave the force of law, but with the addition of the Council of Sar- 
dica, of the so-called Canons of the Apostles, and of Ixviii, canons of St. Basil. 
The full text of all these canons he exhibited ‘not in any chronological order : 
nor according to the sequence of the canons themselves,’ but digested uecord- 
ing to their subject matter under x, Titles. Afterwards, when Patriarch of 
©. P., he added a Second Part—his ‘Nomocanon’ properly so called—which 
consisted of a repetition of the L, Titles with the canons belonging to each 
indicated now only by references, but with extracts subjoined to these references 
under ench Title’ from the Code and Novells of Justinian, And after all he 
appended separately xxi, other extracts from the same Novells not pluced before 
under any one of the L, Titles, 

_As time went on, various supplements were annexed to his work by tran- 
scribers, Such were those extracts from ch. xxxii, xxxili, and xlvi, of lib, viii. 
of tho ‘Apostolical Constitutions’ (not yet proseribed by the C, in Trullo) which 
still make sections I. U1, 1V, of the printed Kormchay ; then, various canons 
of St, Basil and of other Fathers: also one canon of a Council held at C, Py in 
A.D, 394 under Nectarius, concerning the rival claims of Agapius and Gabadius 
to the see of Bostra; and an Account of the Council held at C. 2, in Trullo, in 


A.D. 691, with some of its canons. 
This Council, adding the ‘Canons of the Apostles,’ and those of Sardica and

Carthage, together with many cnnons and writings of St. Basil and other Fa- 
thers, and cii, canons of its own, to that code which had been sanctioned in the 
fifth century at Chalcedon, would have made it necessary 160 years before the 
time of Photius to recast and expand the Nomocanon, But the Council in 
Trullo of A.D, GOT being unconfirmed by the Popes, and having worded some 
canons in a tone offensive to them and tending to schism, could not be put for- 
ward as authoritative, so long as union was preserved with Rome, or so long 
Qs it permanent rupture was not intended. In fact, it was only in A.D, 879, at 
the restoration of Photius, or rather only in A,p, 012, when his name was re- 
inserted in the diptychs, that it was decided synodically to identify the Council 
of A.D. GOL with the Sixth Meum, Council, also held at CLP. and ‘in Trullo? in 
A.D. O80, GSI, Nor could Photius’ second Notmocanon, prepared anonymously, 
after his last deposition in A.D, 586, on the basis of canon ii, of the Council Cin 
Trullo’ of A.D, G91, and taking in not only that council and the Seventh Meum, 
of AD. 787, but also two other local councils of CLP. held under himself, come 
jnto use till after A.D, YL, ’ 

Vhotius, in his yrs¢ edition of the Nomocanon, as is shown by its preface 
(retained, together with the preface to his second edition, in the printed Korm- 
chny), reettst (A.D, 8O8-S66) the Nomocanon of Johannes Scholasticus thus : 

Instead of the L. Titles, he digested the canons, those, that is, of the ten 
Councils of Joh, Scholasticus held before A.b, 553, with those of Carthage of 
A.D. 410 (which he added as containing many things useful, though mixed with 
focal matters and Western customs at variauce with Hastern), and with other

Inthe 15th century the two streams of ecclesinstical and elvil legislation began 
to separate, A separate statute-book (sudebxik) was put out in 1408 by John

Palwologi, adopting the double-headed eagle, and throwing off the Tatar yoke, 
already showed a disposition to lay hands on the property of the Church, but 
was checked by the remonstrances of the metr. Simon (sce Blackmore's //ixt. 
of the Russ, Clarch, p, 92), And in the following century, under John IV, 
Basilievich (A.D. 1583-1584), while the ceclesiastical code (ic, the concord. 
ance of existingspractice with the canons) was revised and set forth in some 
respects more distinctly and fully by the Council of the Hundred Chapters (A.D,

second separate civil code was also drawn up and promulgated (A.D, 1508) for 
the use of all civil tribunals, Both the code of 1408 and this of 1568 distinetly 
recognised the eeclesiastleal jurisdiction in its full former extent, and retained 
to the Chureh generally her exclusive jurisdiction over the laity living on her 
estntes and over many others besides, as orplinns and widows, &e, Still it pre- 
rcribed certain limitations to these privileges, and seta bar, in accordance with 
nr petition from the boyars, to any farther acquisition of landed properties by 
the clergy and monks, though grants and permisslons continued to be made all 
the same by the sovereign himself, 

John IV, in that later part of his reign which has obtained for him the sur- 
name of the Terrible, after causing the metr, Philip to be dragged from the

property (an ukaz of his own also forbidding the sume), and that it should

Blackmore's Jist, of the Duss. Church, p. 120.)

Soon after the accession of Alexis Michaelovich, in A.D, 1648, when he was 
only in his twentieth year, another code was drawn up under the influence of

the clergy themselves, in civil causes, from the least to the grentest : so that at 
this point the civil and the ecclesiastical law, which had already for a century 
and a half been separate the one from the other, began to be at variance, This

sacrosanctis ecclesiis orthodox religtonis retro principes priestiterunt flrmin et

&e. Priedictarnm enim quatuor synodorum dogmata sicut sanctas seripturas 
aecipimnua, et regulas sicut leges observamus,’ 

And in like manner afterwards by the Basilica (lib. v. tit. dif, ch. if.) all 
those canons and canonical writings which were contirmed by canon ii, of the

XLIV, From tit, 1x, ch. xxxvi, ‘In tit. iii, of book xvi, of the Basilica,

This is from the gloss of Zonaras on canon IXxxiv, of the Apostles (fol. 23 
overl. of vol, i, of the Kormchay of 1787, and Bev, i. p. 55), There is one very 
curious error in the printed Kormehay, and xome other errors in the Ms, of 
Nicon’s Replies and in the English translation, which make Nicon’s quotation 
here much less to his purpose than it ought to have been... 6'To reprove him, 
the emperor, when he deserves it, is not forbidden, though the words of reproof, 
if they be very sharp (Spyatrepa bvra), may be taken by him as an insult. To 
reproach him without Just cause is not allowed by the canon, so that it is under- 
stood from the distinction made (as e& dv7tBiactoAts voetaOar) that he who with 
Just cause reproves a king does not deserve ‘punishment.’ In tit. iif, of book 
xvi, of the Basilien, ch, xiii, it is said thus: ‘If any one shall speak evil of the 
emperor, he is of liable to punishment, edy tis Kaxds prnuovedan rod BaciAdws obx 
broxerrat Tinwpla’ but the Kormechay has ‘he és liable to punishment: and the 
ms, of Nicon’s Replies not only has ‘he shall be punished,’ but adds ‘by death 
with tortures, and ne reference ought to be made about him to the emperor ;’ 
though the Kormehay after the word ‘punishment’ has rightly “but a report 
must be made about him to the emperor, lor if he uttered such words of 
folly, he may be despised, but if of madness, he deserves to be pitied, or if he 
did it because he had been wronged, he is to be forgiven.’ 

But the canon to which this gloss of Zonaras is attached in the Earnalisy 
is not the full canon glossed by him, but the short canon used and glossed by 


PART IL, OF THE KORMCHAY. 649 


Aristin, The full canon is, ‘If any one reproaches (Spite) the emperor or a 
ruler without just cause, let him be punished (tipwpiav rwvéirw); and if he be a 
clerk, let him be deposed ; but if a layman, let him be excommunicated.’ The 
true sense of this is not, as Paisius translated it, ‘let him be punished corporally 
and even eapitally, and (besides) Jet him if a clerk be deposed,’ &e., but ‘let 
him be punished if a clerk by deposition, or if a layman by excommunication,’ 
But Aristin’s shortened canon in the Kormehay is, ‘He who reproaches unjustly 
ruler or the emperor, if a clerk is deposed, if a layman is excommunicated ;’ 
which led Nicon into the error of arguing as if the words ‘let him be punished’ 
were not merely mistranslated but added altogether by Paisius,
